overview:
In Jainism, "Bhandaras" (more precisely jñāna-bhaṇḍāras or jñān-bhaṇḍārs) are repositories of sacred and scholarly texts, usually housed in temple complexes or monastic institutions. They function as libraries, archives, and ritual spaces where the written word of the Jinas and later ācāryas is preserved, venerated, and studied. Historically, these bhandaras have been central to the Jain community’s efforts to safeguard scriptural authority after the physical absence of omniscient teachers, and they embody the Jain conviction that right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) is indispensable for liberation.

From at least the early medieval period, Jain communities—both Digambara and Śvetāmbara—developed extensive manuscript collections in palm leaf, birch bark, cloth, and paper. These collections were often established under the guidance of eminent monks and supported by kings, ministers, merchants, and lay devotees. In many regions, especially western India, temple bhandaras became the intellectual heart of Jain life, storing canonical texts, commentaries, philosophical treatises, ritual manuals, narrative literature, and even works from non-Jain traditions such as Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, and Buddhist schools. The result is a manuscript heritage that is not only sectarian but also ecumenical, preserving a wide spectrum of Indian intellectual history.

Ownership and management of bhandaras typically followed the Jain principle of non-possession (aparigraha) at the monastic level. While individual scholars might be associated with particular collections, the manuscripts themselves were understood as belonging to the saṅgha—the local or regional community of monks, nuns, and laity. This collective model allowed broad participation in copying, donating, cataloguing, and safeguarding texts. In times of political unrest, such as invasions or social upheaval, manuscripts were moved from vulnerable centers (for example, Patan and Khambhat) to safer locations like Jaisalmer, where they could be preserved in relative security. In other regions, such as Karnataka, Digambara grantha-bhaṇḍāras remained in situ and continued to grow.

Materially, bhandaras reveal a sophisticated culture of book-making and preservation. Manuscripts were written with great care, proofread (saṃśodhita), and sometimes lavishly illustrated. Special containers (dabdab, bhaṇḍār) and architectural features—vaults, underground chambers, pillars with hidden cavities—were used to protect them from fire, water, insects, and theft. Festivals such as Jñāna Pañcamī and Śruta Pañcamī highlight the ritual dimension of these repositories: manuscripts are ceremonially brought out, cleaned or re-covered, worshipped, and new texts are donated to the temple libraries. In this way, bhandaras are not merely storage spaces but living institutions woven into the rhythm of Jain devotional and educational practice.

Historically important centers include the bhandaras of Patan, Khambhat, and Jaisalmer in western India, as well as numerous Digambara collections in Karnataka and elsewhere. The Hemacandra Jñān Bhandar at Patan, for example, preserves vast numbers of manuscripts that testify to the intense scribal activity of Jain laity and monks. The Jaisalmer bhandara, associated with the Khartaragaccha lineage, contains early palm-leaf manuscripts of key texts like the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya, along with corrected copies of canonical works. Such collections have become indispensable for modern scholarship on Jain history, doctrine, art, and manuscript culture, and they also preserve many non-Jain works that might otherwise have been lost.

In contemporary Jain life, bhandaras continue to serve multiple roles. They are places of study (svādhyāya), where monks, nuns, and lay students engage with canonical and post-canonical literature. They are also sites of ritual, where the worship of knowledge (jñāna-pūjā) is performed through reverence for manuscripts and printed books. At the same time, they pose challenges: conservation of fragile materials, responsible cataloguing, and ethical access for researchers and devotees. Different Jain traditions may emphasize distinct aspects—some focusing more on scriptural preservation, others on temple-centered ritual—but across the spectrum, bhandaras remain a tangible expression of the Jain commitment to safeguarding and transmitting liberating knowledge.

Scholarly discussions note that our understanding of bhandaras is shaped by both traditional narratives and modern manuscript surveys. While there is broad agreement on their importance, details such as the exact number of historical repositories, the dating of specific collections, and the extent of non-Jain materials preserved can vary between sources. Translation of technical terms (for example, jñān-bhaṇḍār vs. grantha-bhaṇḍār) and regional practices also introduces nuance. Nonetheless, the core picture is clear: bhandaras are central institutions in Jainism, linking devotion, learning, and cultural memory through the careful preservation of texts.

primary_sources.title: Prabhāvakacaritra
primary_sources.author: Prabhācandra (Śvetāmbara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text: कुमारपालप्रभुना बहु ग्रन्थप्रति प्रज्ञाचक्षुर्भगवतः हेमचन्द्राचार्यस्य व्याकरणग्रन्थानां प्रचुरं प्रलेखनं कृत्वा तान् विद्वद्भ्यः सर्वतो देशे वितरयामास।
primary_sources.transliteration: kumārapāla-prabhunā bahu grantha-prati prajñā-cakṣur-bhagavataḥ hemacandrācāryasya vyākaraṇa-granthānāṃ pracuraṃ pralekhanaṃ kṛtvā tān vidvadbhyaḥ sarvato deśe vitarayāmāsa.
primary_sources.translation: King Kumārapāla caused numerous copies of the grammar treatises of the venerable Hemacandra, the seer of wisdom, to be written out in great quantity, and he distributed them to learned men in all regions.
primary_sources.notes: This passage, cited in later Jain historical literature, is used to illustrate royal patronage of Jain textual culture and the establishment of large repositories of manuscripts. It supports the tradition that Kumārapāla founded multiple jñān-bhandaras and commissioned extensive copying of Hemacandra’s works. Exact wording varies slightly across editions and translations, and the link between this patronage and specific surviving bhandaras (such as those at Patan) is partly reconstructed from historical inference and manuscript colophons.

primary_sources.title: Kumārpālprabandha
primary_sources.author: Somaprabha (Śvetāmbara narrative literature)
primary_sources.original_text: सिद्धराजजयसिंहे त्रिशतं लेखकान् समाहूय सर्वदर्शनग्रन्थानां लेखनं कारितम्, तैः लिखितानां ग्रन्थानां राजकीयं भण्डारं स्थापयामास।
primary_sources.transliteration: siddharāja-jayasiṃhe triśataṃ lekhakān samāhūya sarva-darśana-granthānāṃ lekhanaṃ kāritam, taiḥ likhitānāṃ granthānāṃ rājīyaṃ bhaṇḍāraṃ sthāpayāmāsa.
primary_sources.translation: King Siddharāja Jayasiṃha summoned three hundred scribes and had them write texts from all philosophical schools; from the manuscripts thus produced he established a royal repository.
primary_sources.notes: This narrative highlights the creation of a large royal library that included Jain and non-Jain works. Jain authors later connect such royal repositories with the broader culture of bhandaras and with Jain efforts to preserve texts of multiple traditions. As with many prabandha sources, the account blends historical memory and literary embellishment, so precise historical details must be corroborated with manuscript evidence and external records.

primary_sources.title: Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (manuscript tradition)
primary_sources.author: Jinabhadragaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa
primary_sources.original_text: णमो अरिहंताणं, णमो सिद्धाणं, णमो आयरियाणं, णमो उवज्झायाणं, णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं।
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ, ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ, ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: Homage to the Arhats, homage to the Siddhas, homage to the Ācāryas, homage to the Upādhyāyas, homage to all the Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: A ninth-century palm-leaf manuscript of this text was discovered in the Jaisalmer jñān-bhaṇḍāra. The presence of such early and carefully corrected manuscripts illustrates the antiquity and scholarly character of Jain bhandaras. While the verse itself is a well-known canonical formula, its manuscript context in Jaisalmer provides concrete evidence of how bhandaras preserved key doctrinal texts over centuries.

primary_sources.title: Śruta-pañcamī and Jñāna-pañcamī ritual manuals (various)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous ritual compilers in Śvetāmbara traditions
primary_sources.original_text: आज श्रुतपञ्चमी महोत्सवे जिनवचनरूप ग्रन्थानां पूजां कुर्मः, तेषां भण्डारस्थापनं च यथाशक्ति साधयामः।
primary_sources.transliteration: āja śruta-pañcamī mahotsave jinavacana-rūpa granthānāṃ pūjāṃ kurmaḥ, teṣāṃ bhaṇḍāra-sthāpanaṃ ca yathā-śakti sādhayāmaḥ.
primary_sources.translation: Today, on the great festival of Śruta-pañcamī, we perform worship of the texts that embody the Jina’s word, and, according to our capacity, we undertake the establishment and support of their repositories.
primary_sources.notes: Ritual texts for Śruta-pañcamī and Jñāna-pañcamī describe the worship of manuscripts and the donation of new texts to temple libraries. While wording differs across regional and sectarian manuals, the core idea is consistent: bhandaras are ritually acknowledged as sacred spaces where the Jina’s teaching is preserved. These sources show how textual preservation is integrated into lay and monastic religious practice, not treated as a purely secular activity.

misconceptions.myth: Bhandaras are simply old storage rooms for outdated manuscripts that no longer have religious significance.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain tradition, bhandaras are revered as living repositories of sacred knowledge. Manuscripts housed there are objects of ritual respect, studied in svādhyāya, and central to festivals such as Śruta Pañcamī and Jñāna Pañcamī. Even when texts are historically or philosophically complex, they remain part of the community’s ongoing engagement with the Jina’s teaching and related intellectual traditions.

misconceptions.myth: Only Jain scriptures are kept in bhandaras; they have no connection to non-Jain philosophies or wider Indian intellectual history.
misconceptions.reality: Many Jain bhandaras preserve a wide range of materials, including works on Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Buddhist philosophy, grammar, astronomy, and other disciplines. Jain patrons and scribes often copied and safeguarded texts from non-Jain schools, so these repositories have become crucial sources for reconstructing broader Indian intellectual history, not just Jain doctrine.

misconceptions.myth: Bhandaras belong exclusively to individual monks or temple authorities and are a form of personal possession.
misconceptions.reality: While particular monks, ācāryas, or temple trusts may administer bhandaras, the collections are traditionally understood as belonging to the saṅgha—the wider community of monks, nuns, and laity. This collective model reflects Jain ideals of non-possession and shared responsibility, and it has historically enabled broad participation in copying, donating, and preserving manuscripts.

misconceptions.myth: Modern printed books have completely replaced bhandaras, making manuscript repositories irrelevant for contemporary Jain practice.
misconceptions.reality: Printed editions have expanded access to Jain texts, but manuscript bhandaras remain vital. They preserve variant readings, commentaries, and works that have never been printed, and they serve as the basis for critical editions and historical research. For many communities, the physical manuscripts also carry ritual and emotional significance that printed books alone cannot replace.
